evidence.exact_quote: Renderer modes, clipboard, IME, accessibility, text/selection model, TUI capture, terminal shortcuts, and requested/effective renderer disclosure remain first-class acceptance requirements across platforms.

items.impact: Renderer implementations must preserve input, accessibility, capture, and honest fallback behavior across every supported mode.
items.statement: The renderer contract makes clipboard, IME, accessibility, Unicode text and selection semantics, TUI capture, shortcuts, and requested/effective disclosure inseparable acceptance concerns.
items.title: Renderer accessibility and text-model matrix

evidence.exact_quote: PM must not mask a remote, WSL, container, or unsupported runtime request by silently launching a local shell or generic GUI fallback.

items.impact: Cross-platform routing remains honest and cannot silently change the execution host or capability class.
items.statement: Legacy routing shorthand is normalized through canonical host and renderer contracts, with silent local or generic-GUI fallback expressly forbidden.
items.title: Platform routing has a no-silent-fallback boundary

evidence.exact_quote: Terminal subsystem architecture has explicit process-host, PTY transport, VT/ANSI grid buffer engine, renderer, shell-integration metadata, and workspace/session UI layers with acceptance gates for platform behavior.

items.impact: Builders must preserve layer boundaries and platform gates instead of merging transport, parsing, rendering, and UI responsibilities.
items.statement: The terminal architecture is a layered contract spanning host, PTY transport, mutable grid engine, renderer, shell metadata, and workspace/session UI.
items.title: Terminal subsystem layer contract

evidence.exact_quote: Terminal parser and replay requirements preserve mutable grid/buffer state, scrollback and selection anchors, command-block annotations, replay fixtures, resize/reflow, huge output, Unicode/IME, search, and TUI capture behavior.

items.impact: Replay fixtures must exercise mutable state and difficult resize, output-volume, input-method, search, and TUI cases.
items.statement: Parser correctness is expected to be replay-testable across grid mutation, scrollback, anchors, annotations, resize/reflow, huge output, Unicode/IME, search, and TUI capture.
items.title: Terminal parser replay coverage

evidence.exact_quote: A DOM-style, document-style, line-widget-per-output, or string-concatenation terminal core is non-ship; terminal output is mutable grid/buffer state rendered by a purpose-built terminal engine.

items.impact: A builder cannot substitute a document or per-line widget model for the required mutable terminal engine.
items.statement: The non-ship boundary unambiguously forbids DOM-style, document-style, per-line-widget, and string-concatenation terminal cores.
items.title: Purpose-built mutable terminal core is mandatory

evidence.exact_quote: Terminal performance requires off-UI-thread PTY and buffer work, diff/dirty-region painting, throttled rendering, bounded memory, stable scroll/selection/focus, and platform performance tests.

items.impact: Without numeric latency, throughput, memory, and stability thresholds, incompatible implementations can all claim to satisfy performance acceptance.
items.statement: The required performance techniques and qualitative outcomes are clear, but bounded memory, responsiveness, throttling, and platform test pass/fail thresholds are not quantified in this unit.
items.title: Terminal performance gates lack measurable thresholds

evidence.exact_quote: Terminal observability records structured lifecycle and state-transition events including create, attach, ready, start/finish command, interrupt, terminate, kill, detach, reattach, move-window, resize, focus/visibility, cwd/profile changes, renderer errors, shell-integration changes, selection/clipboard failures, and capability fallback.

items.impact: Lifecycle, interaction, failure, and fallback state can be diagnosed without scraping rendered output.
items.statement: Terminal observability requires structured events across the complete pane/session lifecycle and the named error and capability transitions.
items.title: Structured terminal lifecycle event surface

evidence.exact_quote: Terminal settings and diagnostics expose renderer mode/fallback, shell-integration capability tier/source, last restore outcome, transcript persistence and retention availability, and recent errors/events relevant to the current pane.

items.impact: Users and support flows can inspect effective capability, restore, retention, and error truth for the active pane.
items.statement: The diagnostics UI must expose effective renderer and shell-integration state plus restore, persistence, retention, and recent-error outcomes.
items.title: Terminal diagnostics disclose effective state

evidence.exact_quote: Terminal diagnostic logging records metadata, state transitions, failure codes, and performance counters without indiscriminate shell-content capture; user-requested diagnostic bundles clearly label transcript content as absent, partial, or included.

items.impact: Diagnostic exports avoid silent shell-content leakage and tell users exactly which transcript class is present.
items.statement: Logging defaults to metadata and counters, while bundles must disclose whether transcript material is absent, partial, or included.
items.title: Terminal diagnostic privacy boundary

evidence.exact_quote: Rollback/snapshot boundaries allow terminal metadata, layout state, settings, and retained transcript artifacts to be snapshotted, but not arbitrary live PTY or process undo after commands have executed.

items.impact: Recovery UX cannot falsely promise undo of side effects already executed by a terminal process.
items.statement: Snapshot scope is limited to restorable structure and retained artifacts; live PTY/process execution is explicitly irreversible.
items.title: Terminal rollback truth is explicit

evidence.exact_quote: Repeated identical terminal failures are coalesced under the /noise rule while persistent degraded state remains inspectable, and major terminal subsystem state is queryable per pane/session and project-wide without scraping rendered UI text.

items.impact: Different event keys, time windows, counters, or retention policies could hide persistent failures or flood diagnostics while still claiming /noise compliance.
items.statement: Queryable state and the need to preserve persistent degradation are clear, but the identity, time-window, count, and reset semantics for coalescing repeated failures are not defined here.
items.title: Terminal noise coalescing needs deterministic semantics

evidence.exact_quote: Terminal acceptance requires deterministic two-section, multi-tab, one-to-four pane behavior across docked/detached presentation, same-session reveal, restart identity minting, honest historical restore, terminal/output/problems/debug/ports linkback, and responsive huge-output/search/scrollback paths.

items.impact: Acceptance must cover layout, identity, restore truth, cross-surface navigation, and high-volume terminal interactions together.
items.statement: The terminal acceptance matrix names the required sections, pane counts, dock states, reveal and restart identity behavior, historical restore truth, linkbacks, and huge-output paths.
items.title: Terminal end-to-end acceptance matrix

evidence.exact_quote: Dev sessions are stack-aware and distinguish hot reload from live reload, with explicit cleanup and termination rules for project switch and app shutdown.

items.impact: Without explicit states and precedence for launch, fallback, switch, shutdown, and cleanup failure, session implementations may diverge or leak processes.
items.statement: The semantic distinction and cleanup triggers are required, but this unit does not define the dev-session transition model or cleanup-failure outcomes.
items.title: Hot/live reload lifecycle remains under-specified

evidence.exact_quote: Hot/live reload UI discloses fallback to live reload, and one-click launch, status, logs, errors, and termination rules are required.

items.impact: Users can distinguish the requested reload mode from fallback and inspect lifecycle status, logs, errors, and termination behavior.
items.statement: The reload UI must disclose fallback and provide launch, status, log, error, and termination surfaces.
items.title: Reload UI must expose effective mode and lifecycle

evidence.exact_quote: Sound effects are grouped settings, not per-view ad hoc toggles, and sound notifications follow action-needed/completion semantics while respecting do-not-disturb or muted-state shell policy.

items.impact: Builders may choose inconsistent events, priorities, and suppression behavior despite the grouped-settings and DND boundaries.
items.statement: Settings ownership and shell mute/DND precedence are clear, but exact action-needed and completion event mapping is left to builder discretion.
items.title: Sound notification event taxonomy is missing

evidence.exact_quote: Instant project switch defaults to switching the active workspace tab, while an alternate command opens the target project in a new workspace tab.

items.impact: Default and alternate commands have distinct, testable workspace-tab effects.
items.statement: Project switch replaces the active workspace-tab project by default; a separate command opens the project in a new workspace tab.
items.title: Project switch command effects are explicit

evidence.exact_quote: Project switching recalculates project-scoped config, sessions, terminal cwd, browser preview state, effective tool/MCP/Persona state, preserves old project background activity through attention surfaces, and exposes deterministic missing-path, duplicate-path, and in-flight-run states.

items.impact: A partially applied switch can mix config, cwd, preview, tools, and persona state or misattribute old-project activity.
items.statement: The propagation targets and edge-state names are comprehensive, but ordering, atomic commit, cancellation, concurrent-switch serialization, and rollback behavior are not defined here.
items.title: Project-switch propagation lacks transaction semantics

evidence.exact_quote: The built-in browser and click-to-context browser-interaction topic is separate from websearch, provider-routed webfetch, site/page reading intents, and Site Reader-only behavior.

items.impact: Browser interaction identity, routing, and UX cannot be collapsed into the web-operation or Site Reader paths.
items.statement: The native visible-browser interaction topic is explicitly distinct from search, provider fetch, page-reading intents, and the reserved Site Reader identity.
items.title: Browser and web-read boundaries are explicit

evidence.exact_quote: Promoted GUI consumes web research activity cards without re-owning tool routing, preserving Searching Web and reserved Reading Site labels, Site Reader detail-level choices, token-efficient fetches, observe/read path separation, and free-tier/provider-limit degradation before unavailable actions.

items.impact: The promoted GUI reflects routing and degradation truth while preserving reserved labels and separate observe/read capabilities.
items.statement: Web-research UI is a consumer of tool activity, not a routing owner, and must disclose detail level and provider/free-tier degradation before actions are offered.
items.title: Web-research activity and degradation UI

evidence.exact_quote: PM browser runtime is capability-first and PM-managed CEF by default; wef, cargo-wef, Wry/hybrid, OS webviews, Playwright/CDP sidecars, chromiumoxide, and Chrome-for-Testing helpers remain candidates or comparison inputs until packaging, update, install, verification, and health strategy is explicit.

items.impact: The default architecture cannot be considered fully buildable until pinned acquisition, verification, update, health, and rollback behavior is selected.
items.statement: CEF is the default design center, but the unit expressly leaves packaging, update, install, verification, and health strategy unresolved and treats multiple helper paths as candidates.
items.title: PM-managed browser runtime strategy remains open

evidence.exact_quote: Browser runtime capability state is requested/effective and must disclose runtime_unavailable, degraded capability, visible-host support, platform differences, and capability-degradation before offering unavailable features.

items.impact: Unavailable or degraded browser features cannot be advertised as if they were fully supported.
items.statement: Browser UX must show requested versus effective state and advertise degradation or runtime unavailability before the user can invoke an unsupported feature.
items.title: Browser capability disclosure is pre-offer

evidence.exact_quote: Browser click, highlight, capture, and share flows use explicit user-triggered chips; cmd.browser.share_with_agent and revoke_share_with_agent update explicit browser-session share state only.

items.impact: Agent browser context is visible, revocable, session-scoped, and cannot be injected invisibly.
items.statement: Only explicit user-triggered chips establish browser context sharing, and share/revoke commands mutate browser-session share state rather than broader hidden context.
items.title: Browser context sharing requires explicit chips

evidence.exact_quote: Browser text selection and element pick create browser_selection_context and browser_element_context chips, while screenshots and combined captures create runtime-artifact references and must not inject raw unbounded page bodies, DOM dumps, or screenshots directly into prompt text.

items.impact: Prompt payloads remain bounded and auditable while large or binary browser captures stay in the artifact pipeline.
items.statement: Selections and elements become typed chips; screenshot-bearing captures become artifact references, never unbounded raw prompt injection.
items.title: Browser prompt attachment boundary

evidence.exact_quote: The browser control plane remains named-action based, covering tab lifecycle, richer interactions, wait primitives, dialogs, file uploads, storage controls, network routing/mocking, trace/video capture, page/PDF export, test verification, coordinate fallback, and locator generation.

items.impact: Named-action scope is broad enough that missing per-action preconditions, outputs, timeouts, idempotence, and partial-failure behavior could yield incompatible control planes.
items.statement: The taxonomy establishes strong named actions and excludes freeform low-level execution, but this unit does not itself define each action's full state, permission, failure, and output semantics.
items.title: Named browser taxonomy needs action-level contracts

evidence.exact_quote: Embedded/detached DevTools, agent/browser introspection, and advanced browser test-debug flows are explicit opt-in or named-action surfaces; raw DevTools/CDP scripting and page-code execution are not the default PM browser contract.

items.impact: Low-level page execution cannot silently become the product's normal agent authority surface.
items.statement: DevTools and test-debug escape hatches are opt-in, while named browser actions remain the guaranteed default contract.
items.title: Raw browser execution is outside the default contract

evidence.exact_quote: Browser screenshots, traces, combined selection/screenshot captures, DevTools automation artifacts, and evidence actions use the runtime-artifact pipeline with naming, retention, manifest shape, chat rendering, privacy redaction, permission disclosure, and requested/effective capability state.

items.impact: If the owner documents do not provide exact manifest, retention, redaction, permission, and rendering rules, browser evidence can leak data or become unrecoverable and nonportable.
items.statement: This unit requires a comprehensive artifact pipeline but delegates the executable field shapes and lifecycle details to referenced owner contracts not present in this source excerpt.
items.title: Browser artifact pipeline depends on external exact contracts

evidence.exact_quote: Browser session persistence covers history, cookies, storage, auth sessions, profile { name, saveChanges }, project-scoped normal sessions, workspace_preview/detached_preview sharing, isolated automation_session and auth_session profiles, restore eligibility, and crash recovery.

items.impact: Ambiguous save, isolation, expiry, crash-recovery, and concurrent-profile semantics can expose credentials or corrupt session state.
items.statement: Profile classes and broad persistence scope are named, but exact saveChanges timing, isolation guarantees, lifecycle/retention, concurrent access, and restore eligibility predicates are not defined here.
items.title: Browser profile persistence requires exact lifecycle rules

evidence.exact_quote: Browser tab-cap handling is no-silent-retargeting/no LRU reuse: PM prompts, blocks, explicitly closes, or opens detached rather than silently retargeting an existing browser subject.

items.impact: Reaching a tab cap cannot silently change an existing browser subject or destroy the user's context.
items.statement: At the tab cap, only explicit prompt, block, close, or detached-open outcomes are allowed; LRU reuse and silent retargeting are forbidden.
items.title: Browser tab-cap behavior preserves subject identity

evidence.exact_quote: PM-managed browser helpers use helper/subprocess lifecycle, crash detection, restart policy, sandboxing, diagnostics, per-platform bundle layout, update rules, signature/hash verification, uninstall/removal evidence, and explicit Linux/macOS/Windows platform guarantees.

items.impact: Security, reliability, rollback, and uninstall behavior remain non-falsifiable until exact signing roots, version policy, restart budgets, layouts, and evidence requirements are specified.
items.statement: Required distribution concerns are exhaustive, but this unit names categories rather than concrete per-platform policies and pass/fail guarantees.
items.title: Browser helper distribution needs concrete policies

evidence.exact_quote: Browser actions, storage/auth use, DevTools flows, artifact capture, agent-vs-user authority, permission keys, trust tiers, auth/session sensitivity, and no-silent-fallback blocked semantics are governed by Permissions and safety contracts.

items.impact: This unit alone cannot determine whether any specific browser action is permitted, requires consent, is blocked, or can use sensitive auth/session state.
items.statement: The authority dimensions and no-silent-fallback rule are explicit, but concrete permission keys, trust-tier decisions, and user-versus-agent transitions reside in external safety contracts.
items.title: Browser authority depends on an external permission matrix

evidence.exact_quote: Browser command/UI surfaces expose inspect, screenshot, DevTools, automation controls, exact browser chrome controls, status indicators, activity disclosure, and scenario-driven acceptance criteria for preview, interaction, screenshots, DevTools, auth, crash recovery, restore, and cross-platform packaging.

items.impact: A broad scenario list without exact inputs and expected outcomes can permit shallow test coverage and misleading status UI.
items.statement: Required controls, indicators, disclosures, and scenario families are identified, but the source unit does not enumerate executable scenario steps or outcome oracles.
items.title: Browser UI test plan remains qualitative

evidence.exact_quote: Playwright MCP, Chrome DevTools MCP, BrowserMCP, Saik0s/mcp-browser-use, browser-use, chromiumoxide, Wry, WebView2, WKWebView, WebKitGTK, OS webviews, CDP sidecars, and MCP config shapes remain reference, comparison, lineage, or background inputs and do not replace PM-owned browser architecture.

items.impact: Reference implementations and legacy platform labels cannot silently become the product architecture or command surface.
items.statement: External browser projects and runtime labels are lineage and comparison material only; PM retains ownership of the browser architecture.
items.title: Browser references do not own product architecture

evidence.exact_quote: The canonical browser action table and output shape preserve action_id, bucket, tier, permission_layer, allowed_session_classes, requested_capabilities, artifacts_emitted, degradation_or_blocking_behavior, user_visible_entry_points, typed output sections, fields, limits, sequential execution, URL validation, and invalid_input errors.

items.impact: Browser actions have a typed, capability- and permission-aware envelope with bounded inputs and explicit degradation or invalid-input behavior.
items.statement: The browser action schema binds identity, tier, permissions, sessions, capabilities, artifacts, degradation, UI entry points, typed outputs, limits, sequencing, and URL validation.
items.title: Canonical browser action envelope

evidence.exact_quote: The UI command catalog exposes stable command families for project switching/open-new-tab, workspace tabs, detached windows, thread context detail, branching, browser controls, terminal actions, dev-session actions, and catalog lifecycle actions.

items.impact: All major promoted surfaces can consume stable command families rather than ad hoc local actions.
items.statement: The catalog must provide stable families spanning project/workspace/window, thread/branch, browser, terminal, dev-session, and catalog lifecycle operations.
items.title: Promoted command-family coverage

evidence.exact_quote: Open in Terminal and Show Terminal normalize to the terminal command family, terminal layout and runtime actions remain separate command categories, and cross-surface reveal commands target canonical identities such as terminal_session_id and dev_session_id rather than freeform labels.

items.impact: Reveal and runtime actions remain deterministic across surfaces and cannot bind to ambiguous labels.
items.statement: Terminal reveal aliases normalize to one family, layout and runtime commands remain distinct, and reveal targets use canonical session identifiers.
items.title: Command categories and reveal identity are canonical

evidence.exact_quote: Project restore uses stable project_id rather than raw path alone, preserving restore semantics as identity-driven runtime state.

items.impact: Moved, aliased, duplicate, or otherwise changing paths cannot silently redefine project identity during restore.
items.statement: Project restore is keyed by stable project_id and explicitly not by path alone.
items.title: Project restore uses stable identity

evidence.exact_quote: Workspace tabs restore independently, and detached windows restore only when their surface class and platform support allow deterministic restoration.

items.impact: Different platforms may restore, omit, or misrepresent detached surfaces inconsistently without a shared support and fallback matrix.
items.statement: Independent workspace-tab restore is clear, but the exact surface-class/platform eligibility predicate and user-visible outcome when restore is unsupported are not defined here.
items.title: Detached-surface restore eligibility is under-specified

evidence.exact_quote: Normal browser tabs restore by project and workspace tab while preserving profile scope; detached normal browsing restores with the originating normal browsing session when supported.

items.impact: Profile or subject state may be silently dropped or mis-scoped when detached restore is unavailable or the originating session cannot be recovered.
items.statement: Restore scope binds normal tabs to project, workspace tab, and profile, but fallback and disclosure for an unsupported or missing originating detached session are not specified here.
items.title: Normal-browser detached restore needs failure semantics

evidence.exact_quote: Auth sessions and automation sessions do not auto-resume active work after restart, and auth_session must not auto-close on presumed success because completion requires explicit user or provider/flow evidence.

items.impact: Restart cannot silently resume privileged work or falsely declare authentication complete from page heuristics.
items.statement: Auth and automation work never auto-resumes after restart, and auth completion requires explicit user or provider/flow evidence rather than inferred success.
items.title: Auth and automation restart boundary

segments.summary: Reviewed renderer, platform-routing, terminal-layer, parser/replay, non-ship architecture, and performance requirements; the material performance gap is the absence of quantitative gates.
Reviewed terminal observability, diagnostics UI/privacy, rollback truth, noise handling, and the end-to-end acceptance matrix; deterministic coalescing semantics remain missing.
Reviewed reload, sound, project-switch, and browser/web-boundary requirements; reload lifecycle and project-switch transaction semantics are the primary adversarial gaps.
Reviewed research UI, browser runtime selection, capability disclosure, explicit chip sharing, and bounded attachments; the runtime distribution and health strategy is expressly unresolved.

Reviewed named browser actions, DevTools boundaries, artifact flow, profile persistence, and tab-cap behavior; action-level, artifact, and profile lifecycle contracts require exact downstream definitions.
Reviewed browser distribution, permissions, UI testing, reference dispositions, and action schema; concrete platform policy, permission matrix, and executable scenario oracles remain the main gaps.
Reviewed promoted command families and identity-driven restore behavior; detached-surface and normal-browser unsupported restore outcomes need deterministic predicates and disclosure.

cross_document_questions: Do the terminal owner contracts define numeric responsiveness, memory, and replay pass/fail gates for the performance matrix?
Where are project-switch ordering, cancellation, atomic commit, rollback, and concurrent-switch rules canonically instantiated?
Do the browser artifact and permission owner documents provide exact manifest, retention, redaction, consent, trust-tier, and blocked-state schemas?
Which canonical matrix defines detached-window and detached-normal-browser restore eligibility and unsupported-outcome disclosure per platform?
